findings.issue: Source simile: spring whose "crystal stream" falls over the ledges; candidate has "dark water spills", changing the image (dark vs crystal).
findings.fix: So the fight went on around the ship of Protesilaus. Meanwhile Patroclus came up to Achilles with tears welling in his eyes, like a spring whose clear water spills down the ledges of a high cliff. Achilles saw him crying and felt sorry for him. He said, “Patroclus, why are you standing there in tears like a silly little girl who runs to her mother and begs to be picked up and carried? She clings to her mother’s dress and holds her back though her mother is in a hurry, and she keeps looking up at her with wet eyes until her mother lifts her. You are shedding tears just like that, Patroclus. Do you have something to tell the Myrmidons, or me? Or have you had news from Phthia that only you know? They tell me that Menoetius son of Actor is still alive, and that Peleus son of Aeacus is still alive among the Myrmidons. We two would grieve bitterly to lose either of them. Or are you mourning for the Argives, and for the way they are being killed at the ships because of their own arrogance? Do not hide anything from me. Say it, so that both of us know.”

findings.issue: Comma splice: "the sheer cliffs gave you life, you are so cruel and hard" (source: "so cruel and remorseless are you").
findings.fix: Then, knight Patroclus, you answered with a deep sigh, “Achilles, son of Peleus, greatest champion of the Achaeans, do not be angry. I weep because of the disaster that has fallen on the Argives. Every man who has been their champion until now is lying at the ships, wounded by sword or spear. Brave Diomedes son of Tydeus has been hit by a spear. Famed Odysseus and Agamemnon have both taken sword wounds. Eurypylus has been struck in the thigh by an arrow. Skilled healers are tending these heroes and curing their wounds. And you, Achilles, are you still so unyielding? May I never carry the kind of rage you carry, to the ruin of your own good name. Who in later stories will speak well of you if you do not save the Argives from destruction now? You have no pity. The knight Peleus was not your father, and Thetis was not your mother. The gray sea bore you and the sheer cliffs gave you life, so cruel and hard are you. But perhaps you are holding back because you know of some oracle, or because your mother Thetis has told you something from the mouth of Zeus. If so, at least send me out, and the Myrmidons with me, in case I can bring the Danaans some relief. And let me wear your armor. The Trojans may take me for you and leave the field, and the hard-pressed sons of the Achaeans can get a chance to breathe. They have hardly had one while fighting. We are fresh, and we could easily drive these tired men back from our ships and tents to their own city.”

findings.issue: Simile opened with added imperative "Think of fierce, ravening wolves"; source is "Even as fierce ravening wolves ... even so did the leaders". The wolf half is kept but the as-when frame is lost.
findings.fix: Meanwhile Achilles went everywhere among the tents and told his Myrmidons to put on their armor. As fierce, ravening wolves feast on a horned stag they have killed in the mountains, with their jaws red with blood, then go in a pack to lap water from a clear spring with their long thin tongues, reeking of blood and slaughter, and know no fear because hunger drives them, in the same way the leaders and counselors of the Myrmidons gathered around the good squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, and Achilles himself stood among them, urging on both men and horses.

In front of them all, two men armed themselves—Patroclus and Automedon—two men with one mind, to lead the Myrmidons. Then Achilles went into his tent and opened the lid of the strong chest that silver-footed Thetis had given him to take on board ship, and had filled with shirts, cloaks against the cold, and good thick rugs. In this chest he kept a cup of rare workmanship. No man but himself might drink from it, and he made offerings from it to no god except father Zeus. He took the cup from the chest and cleansed it with sulphur. Then he rinsed it in clean water, washed his hands, and drew wine. He stood in the middle of the court and prayed, looking toward heaven and pouring out the wine as a drink offering. Zeus, whose joy is in thunder, did not fail to see him. “King Zeus,” he cried, “lord of Dodona, god of the Pelasgi, you who live far away and rule wintry Dodona, where your prophets the Selli live around you with unwashed feet and beds made on the ground—you heard me when I prayed to you before, and honored me by sending disaster on the Achaeans. Now grant me the fulfillment of one more prayer. I will stay here where my ships are lying, but I am sending my comrade into battle at the head of many Myrmidons. Grant, all-seeing Zeus, that victory goes with him. Put your courage into his heart, so that Hector learns whether my squire is man enough to fight alone, or whether his might is unbeatable only when I myself enter the turmoil of war. Afterward, when he has driven the fighting and the battle cry away from the ships, grant that he returns unharmed, with his armor and his comrades, fighters in close combat.”

findings.issue: Closing of simile garbled: "As that is the earth in such a storm, so great was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses" (source: "even such was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses in their flight").
findings.fix: Patroclus kept steering his horses toward wherever he saw the most men fleeing in confusion, cheering on his men as he went. Chariots were being smashed in all directions, and many a man tumbled from his own car and fell beneath the wheels of Patroclus’s chariot. Its immortal horses, which the gods had given to Peleus, sprang over the trench in a single bound as they raced on. Patroclus was set on getting near Hector, for he had his heart fixed on spearing him, but Hector’s horses were now hurrying him away. The whole dark earth bows before a tempest on an autumn day, when Zeus rains his hardest to punish men who give crooked judgments in their courts, drive justice out of them and ignore the decrees of heaven. All the rivers run full, the torrents tear many a new channel as they roar headlong from the mountains to the dark sea, and it goes badly for the works of men. Such was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses in their flight.
